title: 2026-11-12 p99/p95 latency deep dive with Sigma Robotics
summary: Deep technical session focused on tail latency (p95/p99) for Sigma's inference path; covered streaming vs non-streaming behavior, KV cache effectiveness, batching strategies, quantization tradeoffs, and VPC/on-prem network hops. Agreed next steps: Redwood to share benchmark configs and run a 72-hour pilot with representative traffic; Sigma to provide VPC access details and production traffic profile.
topics: KV cache behavior and cold starts
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-11-12 14:30 UTC | Duration: ~54m | Attendees: Alex Patel (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (CTO Sigma), Maya Chen (Lead ML), Samir Gupta (Infra), Lena Ortiz (Product)

[00:00] Alex Patel: hey everyone thanks for joining, we'll do a deep dive into p95/p99 tail latency for your inference path. i've got priya from the SE team and we'll try to map out where the biggest tail hits are.
[00:12] Jordan Lee: thanks Alex, yeah our SLO today is 99th under 400ms for short-form responses, but in practice p99 spikes to 900ms on busy hours, so that's... uh, painful.
[00:25] Priya Nair: ok that's helpful, quick question — are those numbers for streaming responses or full response (non-streaming)?
[00:33] Maya Chen: mostly non-streaming today; we use our own proxy that buffers until the full response is ready, we tried streaming but it broke some of our client logic.
[00:45] Samir Gupta: also we run in our VPC, traffic goes through our ingress loadbalancer -> envoy -> natgw -> redwood private endpoint via vpn tunnel, so multiple network hops.
[00:58] Alex Patel: perfect, that'll matter. high-level: tail latency can come from three buckets — runtime scheduling (batching contention, KV cache misses), model compute (quantization degred., attention kernel slow paths), and networking (hops, TCP warmups, TLS handshakes).
[01:15] Priya Nair: to add — streaming can improve perceived latency because tokens stream earlier, but it doesn't magically fix p99 if the first-token time is dominated by a cache miss or a cold kernel compile.
[01:30] Jordan Lee: when you say cache miss, you mean the KV cache for context reuse? we have a lot of short-turn conversations where prefix overlap is high, we thought KV cache would help a lot.
[01:40] Priya Nair: yes, KV cache helps when requests share prefixes or when you do multi-turn chats and re-use the KV state. But things that kill p99 are often cold KV caches (evictions) or when batching delays some requests waiting for others — so a tail request waits in queue for the batch to fill.
[01:58] Maya Chen: hmm batching delay — can we cap maximum batch wait? we saw some requests wait up to 150ms for batch formation.
[02:06] Priya Nair: absolutely, Redwood has continuous batching with configurable max wait (ms) and max batch size; you can tune for latency SLOs by lowering wait or forcing smaller max batch sizes at cost of throughput.
[02:18] Alex Patel: also worth noting quantization interplay — int8/4-bit reduces GPU time but sometimes increases variance (long tails) on some kernels; our runtime can select kernels per model profile to reduce that.
[02:32] Samir Gupta: you mentioned kernel selection — does that mean there are compile steps that can block requests? we saw occasional 200-300ms spikes during deploys.
[02:41] Priya Nair: yes, sometimes when a new model variant is loaded, JIT/compile or kernel warmup happens. we try to pre-warm on dedicated capacity or use precompiled variants in hosted, but on private/VPC installs you'll need to ensure nodes are warm or allow graceful warming.
[02:55] Jordan Lee: network again — our path has 3 hops plus the vpn tunnel; is TLS negotiation happening per request? we use keepalives but not always effective on mobile clients.
[03:07] Alex Patel: long-lived TLS sessions and connection pooling reduce that; also streaming uses HTTP/2 persistent streams which helps. But if your client opens many short lived connections, you pay handshakes.
[03:20] Lena Ortiz: question on streaming vs non-streaming: if we enable streaming, do we lose determinism for downstream processing? our analytics pipeline expects a single final payload.
[03:29] Priya Nair: you can do hybrid — stream to end-user but still write the final assembled response back to your analytics endpoint. Redwood can emit both streaming and a final event.
[03:40] Speaker 1: (murmur)
[03:44] Jordan Lee: can you walk through a concrete example of p99 from a KV miss + batching? like a timeline?
[03:50] Priya Nair: sure — imagine req A arrives, cache cold, so the runtime must run full attention compute; req B arrives 10ms later and is batched with A, because max wait is 50ms. If B is quick and A is slow, both get the same compute time but A suffers extra queuing. If the cache had the prefix, the per-request compute would be smaller and queuing less likely. So p99 shows up when rare cache miss + batch assembly + maybe a kernel slow path coincide.
[04:25] Maya Chen: ok, makes sense. have you seen cases where turning down batch size actually improved p99 even though throughput dropped?
[04:32] Priya Nair: yes, especially for bursty workloads. Lowering max batch wait to 10ms + max batch size to small values reduces queuing, which flattens the tail. Redwood Optimize can recommend these settings based on your request distribution.
[04:47] Alex Patel: we should capture your qps distribution and token length distribution; that will let us recommend batching/warmup config.
[04:55] Jordan Lee: our median request is ~80 tokens, 90th ~210 tokens, spikes to 1k+. QPS average is 120 during working hours, but bursts to 350 for short windows.
[05:08] Samir Gupta: also we have a dedicated cluster for other workloads; could that cause noisy neighbors on network?
[05:12] Priya Nair: yes, network saturation and NIC oversubscription can add tail. On private infra ensure dedicated NIC lanes or isolate model-serving instances.
[05:20] Alex Patel: let's talk numbers: you mentioned 900ms p99 — where is the time spent in traces? do you have per-segment breakdown?
[05:27] Jordan Lee: our traces show 120ms on client side (parsing), 70ms on LB, 360ms in our proxy/envoy plus 200ms in the remote runtime, rest are TLS. But these traces are sampled so noisy.
[05:41] Priya Nair: that envoy time seems high — is there any downsampling or rate limiting? Also do you coalesce requests at edge?
[05:48] Jordan Lee: we do some batching at the edge for sys commands, but mostly no.
[05:52] Maya Chen: regarding quantization — can Redwood run model A in 4-bit safely? our quality metric (ROUGE-like) drops ~0.5 points when we tried int4 in house.
[06:02] Priya Nair: model dependent — for many LLMs, int8 or quantized 4-bit with good calibration preserves most quality for generation, but for some tasks (summarization/factuality) you might see degradation. Redwood's platform supports A/B by routing a fraction to higher-precision variants to measure regressions.
[06:18] Jordan Lee: how do you measure p99 for streaming? since streaming yields earlier tokens, how to compute p99?
[06:24] Alex Patel: good point — two metrics: time-to-first-token (TTFT) and time-to-last-token (TTLT). For perceived latency, TTFT p99 matters. For completion SLOs you look at TTLT. Streaming usually reduces TTFT; TTLT still depends on total token generation.
[06:40] Lena Ortiz: curious about KV cache size — our turn history is long (up to 20 turns), will KV cache blow memory?
[06:46] Priya Nair: cache policies are LRU with soft eviction; you can pin frequently used prefixes, snapshot and restore between instances in dedicated mode, and set TTLs. For long histories we often store compressed KV pages and prune non-critical tokens.
[06:59] Samir Gupta: on the VPC network side, our traffic to Redwood Private goes over an IPsec tunnel. There have been jitter spikes — do you support colocated private connectors to reduce hops?
[07:09] Alex Patel: yes, for enterprise private we offer a VPC peering and direct connect option which reduces NAT and VPN overhead; on-prem install avoids tunnels entirely but needs bandwidth.
[07:18] Jordan Lee: if we move to dedicated capacity with pre-warm, can that eliminate kernel warmups? we saw 200ms compile spikes.
[07:25] Priya Nair: dedicated capacity lets you pin model variants and pre-warm kernels; we also provide precompiled kernels for common model families to avoid first-request compilation. That often removes those 100-300ms spikes.
[07:36] Maya Chen: any guidance on max_batch_size vs max_wait for our profile?
[07:41] Priya Nair: rough starting point: for qps 120 median tokens 80, try max_batch_size 8-16 and max_wait 10-25ms. For bursts, enable dynamic overflow where excess requests go to a fast-fail path or smaller batch pool. We'll run a sim with your trace to refine.
[07:58] Jordan Lee: can you talk about connection pooling and client SDK options? we use mobile clients and some server-side callers.
[08:05] Alex Patel: server -> use persistent HTTP/2 and gRPC pools; mobile -> use tokenized edge or a sidecar that pools connections. SDKs can provide automatic retries and connection reuse. Also, prefer HTTP/2/3 where possible.
[08:19] Samir Gupta: what's the impact of TLS handshakes on p99 for many short-lived connections?
[08:24] Priya Nair: TLS adds 50-150ms per handshake depending on network; persistent sessions reduce that. Also TLS 1.3 + session resumption plus caching reduces overhead.
[08:34] Speaker 1: (crosstalk)
[08:38] Alex Patel: ok let's look at an action path: Redwood will run a bench with three scenarios — 1) current config mirrored, 2) tuned batching + continuous caching, 3) quantized int8 variant with A/B. We'll measure p50/p95/p99, TTFT, TTLT, and cost.
[08:55] Maya Chen: sounds good. for the benchmark, we can provide a 72-hour traffic dump and a VPC test endpoint.
[09:03] Priya Nair: perfect — also we'll share our recommended runtime config and a short doc on how to enable streaming safely.
[09:11] Jordan Lee: what about observability — will we get token-level latency breakdown?
[09:15] Alex Patel: yes Redwood Console includes token-level timing, per-model route dashboards, and trace hooks so you can map request through your proxy into runtime.
[09:24] Samir Gupta: one more infra question — if we host on-prem what's the recommended NIC and GPU configuration to avoid tail from PCIe/IO?
[09:32] Priya Nair: generally prefer NVLink connected GPUs for large models, 100Gbps network with SR-IOV or dedicated NICs, and avoid oversubscription on the host. Also tune IRQ affinity and disable unnecessary CPU power saving.
[09:47] Jordan Lee: any gotchas with KV cache and snapshot restore after node restart? we saw cache cold after rolling updates.
[09:54] Alex Patel: you can persist snapshots to S3-compatible storage and restore during node bootstrap; for Dedicated we can orchestrate a staggered rollout to keep snapshots warm.
[10:05] Maya Chen: we tried 4-bit quant and saw hallucination rate increase in some prompts; how do you run quality gating for canary?
[10:13] Priya Nair: Redwood Optimize lets you define eval suites; we run A/B with automatic regressions alerts on chosen metrics (accuracy, hallucination proxies). If drop exceeds threshold we auto-fallback to higher-precision variant.
[10:26] Lena Ortiz: are there any open-source tools or scripts you share for load generation and trace correlation?
[10:31] Alex Patel: yes we'll send a benchmark harness (k6 + custom tokenized workload) and a trace correlation script that maps client request IDs to Redwood trace IDs.
[10:39] Jordan Lee: ok what's the timeline for pilot? we want in 2 weeks.
[10:43] Alex Patel: we can start in 2 weeks pending VPC access; typical pilot is 48-72hrs of representative traffic. We'll need: sample traces, VPC endpoint details, and a CRM PO if private connectivity required.
[10:55] Samir Gupta: security/compliance — we need SOC2 docs and SSO config for Redwood team access to the test cluster.
[11:02] Priya Nair: will share SOC2 and SAML SSO docs. For private we support customer-managed KMS and audit logs.
[11:11] Maya Chen: any final tips to quickly reduce p99 before pilot?
[11:14] Priya Nair: yes — turn on connection pooling, cap max_batch_wait to 10-20ms, enable KV cache for common prefixes, and route very large token requests to a separate queue to avoid blocking short ones.
[11:29] Alex Patel: recap — Redwood will: 1) share benchmark harness + recommended runtime configs, 2) run pilot with three scenarios and deliver p50/p95/p99 + TTFT/TTLT breakdown, 3) provide SOC2/SAML docs. Sigma will: 1) provide traffic dump and VPC test endpoint, 2) share token length distribution and peak QPS windows, 3) confirm pilot start date.
[11:50] Jordan Lee: good recap. thanks everyone.
[11:54] Alex Patel: thanks all, we'll follow up in email with artifacts and schedule.

Notes on transcript quality: some words (e.g., KV cache) may be transcribed as "K-V cash" or "KV cash" in places; speaker labels may be approximate.
